column6: The commentary glosses h-d-y as showing someone both the road and the house. Abraham's servant says that God led him on the road to his master's kinsmen's house, giving the journey image a concrete destination.
YHWH goes before Israel in cloud and fire expressly to lead them on the road. This closely supplies the commentary's claim that the guide is named for advancing ahead of the travelers.
The promised messenger is sent before Israel to guard the way and bring them to a prepared place. It joins the commentary's forward guide, safe route, and arrival.
God goes ahead on Israel's way to seek a place to camp and shows them which route to take. The text makes the guide's prior movement and knowledge of resting place explicit.
The commentary contrasts an unhurried, composed walk with fleeing. Isaiah says the departing people will neither leave in haste nor flee because YHWH goes before them and guards behind.

The commentary's hadi goes ahead and the animal follows readily. Jesus' shepherd goes before his sheep, and they follow because they know his voice, a close Christian pastoral rendering of both actions.
Zechariah's prophecy says the divine visitation will guide feet into the way of peace. It turns the commentary's road-leading and calm gait into an explicitly salvific destination.

When a traveler turns right or left, Isaiah's voice says, "This is the way; walk in it." That is a precise counterpart to the commentary's guide who identifies a road rather than merely giving advice.
God leads blind people on unfamiliar roads and makes rough places level. This combines the commentary's guided traveler with its concern for a route made passable.
The commentary dwells on a long mountain ridge whose climb is made easier. Isaiah's preparation of the divine way lowers mountains, raises valleys, and smooths rough ground.
Baruch says God orders mountains lowered and valleys filled so Israel can walk safely. Its return procession makes the commentary's high route and divinely eased walking a single scene.
Luke applies the leveling of valleys, mountains, crooked places, and rough roads to the coming salvation. It gives a Christian reception of the terrain that the commentary reads as a journey.
God leads Israel through the depths like a horse in the wilderness so that it does not stumble. This directly links the commentary's guided animal and its light, sure movement.
Habakkuk says God makes his feet like a deer's and lets him tread on high places. It is a compact analogue to the commentary's light legs and mountain-ridge travel.
Wisdom's path leaves the walker's stride unconfined and prevents stumbling even when running. It concretizes the commentary's easy road and untroubled gait.

The commentary imagines a horse that yields easily and follows quickly. Psalm 32 warns against an uncomprehending horse or mule that must be restrained by bit and bridle, an instructive inverse image of responsive guidance.
James puts bits in horses' mouths so that they obey and their whole bodies are guided. Its explicit horse, obedience, and direction closely illuminate the commentary's easy-to-lead mount.

The commentary gives the secondary image of a weakened person sustained between two people. Aaron and Hur support Moses' heavy hands from either side, supplying a concrete biblical pattern of two-sided aid to weakness.
The commentary's route concerns weak movement and a path made easy. Hebrews orders straight paths for the feet so that what is lame is healed rather than put out of joint.
Moses' work is too heavy alone, and shared judgment will make it easier for him. This provides a narrative analogue to the commentary's ease as the removal of disabling strain.

column5: guide who knows the road to Media
column6: Tobiah seeks a companion who knows the road, and Raphael assures him that he knows it from repeated travel. The scene gives the commentary's forward guide a named journey companion and a known destination.

After the heavenly encounter leaves Saul unable to see, his companions lead him by hand to Damascus. It offers a concrete Christian counterpart to the commentary's weakened traveler needing bodily guidance.

The commentary turns the promise of ease into a rider-and-mount picture. The Samaritan places the wounded traveler on his own animal and conveys him to care, making the animal an instrument of supported passage.

column5: donkey turns aside before the angel
column6: The commentary reads the wretched person's tajannub as passing the warning by and keeping it at the roadside. Balaam's donkey turns aside from the road because it sees the armed divine messenger that its rider misses; here the sideways movement is the faithful response to warning.

YHWH tells the people to stand at the roads, ask for the good ancient path, walk it, and find rest; they answer that they will not walk in it. This is a close counterpart to the reminder that the wretched person avoids.
Those addressed refuse to heed, turn a rebellious shoulder, and make their ears heavy. The bodily turning away makes unusually concrete the commentary's interpretation of avoiding the reminder.

In Luke's explanation, seed beside the road is the word heard and then removed before belief. It gives the commentary's image of keeping the admonition at one's roadside an explicit parabolic setting.

Hebrews repeats the summons to hear God's voice today and not harden the heart. It places the commentary's contrast between fruitful reminder and wretched avoidance in an exhortatory Christian reception.
Isaiah makes dry grass and stubble burn because the people rejected YHWH's instruction. It binds the commentary's pasture becoming refuse to its adjacent scene of admonition refused and fire.

The commentary's pasture ends as ghutha, expendable dark refuse. Psalm 1 gives the wicked the specific image of chaff driven away, adding an ethical use of agricultural residue without equating the texts.
The pasture in the commentary is brought forth and then becomes dark waste. Isaiah's grass withers and flower fades when the breath of YHWH blows on it, a close vegetation-to-decay image.

James describes the sun's scorching rise: grass withers, its flower falls, and its beauty perishes. This supplies a Christian moral use of the transience visually developed in the commentary's pasture.
The commentary places ghutha beside the wretched person's great fire. Matthew's winnowing scene gathers chaff and burns it, giving an eschatological continuation to that agricultural residue.

The commentary explicitly reads Adam's expulsion from the garden as entry into shaqa, hardship. Genesis curses the ground for Adam and makes his eating depend on toil, the matching narrative consequence.
Genesis sends Adam out of Eden to till the ground from which he was taken. This supplies the expulsion-and-labor scene behind the commentary's Adamic account of hardship.

column5: Abraham saddles a donkey for the journey
column6: The commentary's rider-and-mount imagery ends by invoking Abraham's plea against idols. Genesis shows Abraham rising, saddling his donkey, and setting out, furnishing a literal Abrahamic journey without identifying its purpose with the Qur'anic prayer.

The commentary contrasts the wretched person who keeps the reminder at a distance with Abraham's request to be kept from idols. Isaiah commands defiling and casting away idol-images as something unclean.
Joshua commands Israel to put away the foreign gods among them and incline the heart to YHWH. It makes the commentary's requested separation from idolatry an enacted turn of direction.
The Thessalonians turn to God from idols to serve the living and true God. That conversion gives a New Testament counterpart to Abraham's desire that he and his sons be kept from idol worship.
Paul's direct command to flee idolatry supplies a Christian imperative for the commentary's inverted use of janb: deliberate distance from the false object rather than distance from divine reminder.

This midrash expands Abraham's anti-idolatry into the episode of smashing Terah's images. It gives Jewish narrative force to the commentary's Abrahamic request for separation from idols, while remaining an interpretive tradition rather than a shared biblical scene.

Jubilees portrays Abram burning the house of idols and the resulting crisis in Terah's household. The expansion makes active rupture with idols the narrative counterpart to the commentary's Abrahamic prayer for protection from them.

column5: creation by measure number and weight
column6: The commentary begins with the Creator who creates and proportions. Wisdom says God arranged all things by measure, number, and weight, a particularly exact Jewish articulation of ordered creation.
God asks who fixed the earth's measures and stretched a line over it. It supplies a biblical cosmic instance of the measuring and proportioning named in the commentary on 87:2–3.

column5: weight for wind and measure for waters
column6: Job describes God assigning weight to wind and measure to waters. This makes the commentary's divine measuring a material ordering of a world through which creatures travel.

The Two Spirits Treatise says that God made humanity and appointed two spirits for people to walk by until visitation. It is an unusually close Second Temple analogue to the commentary's created traveler facing divergent roads.

column5: two ways of life and death
column6: The Didache opens with two ways, one of life and one of death. Its explicit road-formulation belongs beside the commentary's one route whose ends become ease or hardship.

column5: way of light and way of darkness
column6: Barnabas introduces two ways of teaching and authority, light and darkness. This Christian two-way schema sharpens the commentary's moral split between following guidance and moving away from warning.
Matthew contrasts the broad way that leads to destruction with the life-giving entrance. It gives a concrete New Testament road division for the commentary's opposed courses of ease and hardship.

The commentary can picture the difficult side as the road of wretchedness, while Matthew calls the life-giving way constricted and hard. The contrary assignment of difficulty makes the comparison interpretively useful rather than a simple equation.

column5: narrow path between fire and water
column6: 4 Ezra imagines the entrance to a city as a single narrow path between fire and deep water. Its perilous route makes the commentary's ridge, choice, and final destination into a vivid Jewish apocalyptic travel scene.

column5: life and death set before a person
column6: Sirach sets life and death before human beings and says each receives what is chosen. It provides a wisdom-text counterpart to the commentary's guided road that divides according to the traveler's response.

column5: yoke of Torah and released burdens
column6: Avot says accepting the yoke of Torah removes other yokes, while throwing it off brings them on. This rabbinic interpretation makes the commentary's ease and hardship consequences of what one willingly follows.
The commentary's yusr is ease, compliant following, and light movement. Jesus calls his yoke easy and burden light, a direct Christian moral use of ease in animal-yoke imagery.

Acts calls a disputed yoke one that neither ancestors nor present hearers could bear. In contrast to the commentary's mount readily yielding to its rider, this verse tests which religious burden is actually bearable.

God promises to put his spirit within Israel and cause them to walk in his statutes. It supplies a biblical model of divine enablement for the commentary's promise to make a person ready for the easy course.

column5: highway on which travelers do not stray
column6: Isaiah's holy highway is a route on which even inexperienced travelers do not go astray. It joins the commentary's explicit guiding with a road made reliable for its walkers.

column5: straight way to an inhabited town
column6: God leads wandering people by a straight way until they reach an inhabited town. Like the commentary's road-and-house gloss, its guidance ends in arrival and habitation.
God promises to make a way in wilderness and rivers in desert. This develops the commentary's divine route-making where the natural terrain itself offers no easy passage.

The Spirit is said to guide the disciples into all truth. It transfers the commentary's guide who shows the road into a Christian account of revelatory direction, rather than treating guidance as mere locomotion.
The commentary moves from pasture to guided travel. Psalm 23's shepherd restores life and guides on right tracks, keeping pasture and route together in a single pastoral image.

column5: ascending mountain to learn God's paths
column6: Nations go up YHWH's mountain so that he may teach them his ways and they may walk in his paths. It connects the commentary's mountain ascent with instruction that directs walking.

After the road-to-house guidance of the same narrative, Rebekah and her companions mount camels and follow the servant. It supplies a literal caravan version of the commentary's rider, animal, and following image.

column5: idols concealed in a camel saddle
column6: The commentary links a camel-hump covering for riding with Abraham's plea to be kept from idols. Rachel hides household gods in a camel saddle and sits on it, a concrete inverse scene in which idolatry is carried inside the riding equipment.

column5: riding on the heights of the land
column6: God makes Israel ride on the heights of the land. It is a poetic counterpart to the commentary's mount and elevated ridge, though it does not itself explain the ease of ascent.
Isaiah calls the righteous person's path level and says the Upright One makes it even. This adds a moral use of levelness to the commentary's easier, balanced road.
The commentary's good hedy is not a fleeing rush. Isaiah says the one who trusts will not act in haste, giving calm movement a faith-based interpretation.
Proverbs warns that haste of feet makes a person miss the way. It provides a compact wisdom counterpoint to the commentary's measured, unhurried gait.

column5: walking backward after refusing to hear
column6: Jeremiah says the people did not listen, walked in their own counsels, and went backward rather than forward. It makes the commentary's contrast between a forward guide and avoidance of admonition spatially explicit.

column5: the two ways and the wicked's end
column6: Psalm 1 contrasts the way known by YHWH with the way of the wicked that perishes. It is a foundational but less pictorial parallel to the commentary's road whose result depends on the traveler.
Moses sets life and death, blessing and curse before Israel and calls for choosing life. It provides covenantal language for the commentary's opposed outcomes of a shown way.

column5: wicked path as darkness and stumbling
column6: The wicked walk in darkness and do not know what makes them stumble. It complements the commentary's wretched traveler with a path whose very obstacles are unrecognized.
The Testament of Asher describes two ways and corresponding dispositions and outcomes. It is a Jewish para-scriptural development of the moral road division in the commentary.

Sirach urges the learner to put neck and shoulder under Wisdom's yoke, which becomes an ornament. It complicates the commentary's easy animal image by treating willingly borne discipline as the route to a good end.
The commentary's weak walker is sustained by others and its easy route relieves hardship. Paul commands mutual burden-bearing, an ethical counterpart without the travel scene itself.

The commentary treats turning aside from the true reminder as the wretched response. Jesus' sheep flee a stranger precisely because they do not know that voice, showing that withdrawal is right or wrong according to the guide recognized.
Christ leaves an example so believers may follow in his steps. This is a Christian ethical use of the commentary's following-behind-a-guide image, without its animal figure.

column5: Lamb shepherding and guiding to waters
column6: The Lamb shepherds the redeemed and guides them to springs of living water. It reverses ordinary rider-and-animal roles while retaining the commentary's leading figure and safe destination.

column5: tormented man sees the blessed afar
column6: The commentary's wrong road culminates with a blessed person looking down to a companion in hell's center. Luke reverses the viewpoint: a tormented rich man sees Abraham and Lazarus far away, a related but differently arranged afterlife sightline.

column5: Balaam as one leaving the straight way
column6: Second Peter calls corrupt teachers people who leave the straight way and follow Balaam's way. Read beside Numbers 22:23, it turns the donkey-and-road episode into a Christian moral warning relevant to the commentary's guidance and wrong turning.

column5: Hebrew shavah and the source label sawa
column6: The commentary explicitly gives سوى the sense of equality and a balanced middle. Isaiah uses Hebrew שוה, a likely Semitic cognate, for being equal or comparable to the Holy One; its context checks the equality sense while supplying no camel-saddle image.
